FREE STATE HEALTH CRISIS II

By: Este de Klerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
When in an accident on the N3 or N5, you will be taken to the Thebe Hospital in Harrismith, medical aid or not. But how equipped is the ambulance that will take you there and the casualty unit?

Summary:
The Free State Department of Health is in a state of collapse. With the MEC of Health in the province boasting that patient care and the safety of patient are his number one priority, patients and doctors on the ground disagree. What they see and experience is not at all the view that the MEC has of what is going on his own department.

When in an accident on the N3 or N5, you will be taken to the Thebe Hospital in Harrismith, medical aid or not. But how equipped is the ambulance that will take you there and the casualty unit at Thebe Hospital where you need to be stabilised or treated?

It is the only hospital in a 80km radius, yet it is still only a district hospital - with no CT scanner. Our source says he prays that he never has to land up in that hospital.

We also again turn our focus to the Free State Health Department's finances - how much wasteful expenditure was there in 2014/2015? And what does the MEC plan to do about the cash-strapped department that doesn't have enough money to provide medicine and basic consumables or cannot repair equipment or infrastructure at failing state hospitals in the province?

Further information:
On Tuesday, MEC Benny Malakoane will deliver his 2015/2016 budget vote speech in the FS legislature. He will say what his plans for the new year are and questions will be asked from the opposition as to how he plans to fix certain problems. The self-confident MEC that said to us he doesn't need someone else to blow his horn, he will do it himself, has some answering to do.

His department was found unfit to manage its own finances last year and the management of the financial part of the department was handed over to the Treasury.

In this story, we will also go back to all three the hospitals we visited, including Dihlabeng and Pelenomi. The Public Service Commission has just finished an investigation into Pelenomi Hospital and found the the hospital needs at least R100 million immediately to just fix the current problems. It has also found that only 5% of the total financial budget in 2014/15 was spent on actual health care and 95% on salaries. The generators was installed in 1955 and the commissioner of the investigation fears that with constant load shedding the hospital will soon be out of a power back-up. The boilers that warms up the water, was installed in 1995 and only has a life span of 15 years. The hospital has not had hot water for more than a year.

Yet, the MEC claims all is well in his department and in his hospitals.

Press Release:


Free State Health Care II
With a shortage of even the most basic medical supplies, the Harrismith ambulance service struggles to save lives. Pelomoni hospital in Bloemfontein is severely cash-strapped and needs R100-million just to fix urgent problems. But the MEC of Health claims all is well in his department. Carte Blanche unearths more evidence of the shocking decline of the Free State health sector.
Watch the clip.


Script:



FREE STATE HEALTH CRISIS II

PRODUCER: ESTE DE KLERK

It’s one of the busiest roads in South Africa: the N3 highway to Durban.
Thousands travel this route from Gauteng through the Free state to Kwazulu-Natal and back all year round and hundreds of people lose their lives here.

During Easter weekend last year, more than 900 vehicles per hours travelled on this route passing Harrismith.

DR. BRYCE WICKHAM: Whether you have a medical aid or not, if you have an accident more or less within a 80km radius on the N3, on the N5 of Harrismith, you are going to Thebe Hospital.

Dr. Bryce Wickham worked at Thebe as a medical officer for three years before resigning last year.

DR. BRYCE WICKHAM: I would not put my life in the hands of this hospital, not in a million years, not in its current state.

Without a fully equipped trauma unit, Dr. Wickham believes Thebe cannot provide adequate care for road accident victims.

DR. BRYCE WICKHAM: It would need a CT scanner, at least a blood bank, a laboratory, more beds, specialized medical services, specialists in their fields, at least an orthopaedic surgeon, a general surgeon, an anaesthetist, none of which are available at Thebe Hospital.

From the accident scene you will most likely be rushed to Thebe by a Free State provincial ambulance.

RAMCHINDAR SEWPERSAD: There is no time to stay and play, sometimes it is just load and go. You call for back-up sometimes.

Ramchindar Sewpersad, who’s been base in Harrismith for the past three years, says their ambulances often have to call for back-up due to a dire shortage of essential life-saving supplies. He’s been an emergency care worker for 29 years experience.

RAMCHINDAR SEWPERSAD: I feel helpless and hopeless sometimes, because a mechanic cannot work on a car without his tools. When I worked on the ambulance, it was frightening to see that at that stage there were no drips, there were no administration sets, there were no lancets, there was no oxygen, there were no electrodes for the ECG monitor.

He says about 95% of the emergency workers in Harrismith have only received basic ambulance training.

RAMCHINDAR SEWPERSAD: They need intense help and we need more intermediate crews who can put up drips and things like that, they don’t do that, they don’t use an ECG monitor.

In 2007, Christa and Nick Manias’s friends were involved in an accident near the Sterkfontein Dam. Christa and Nick were on the scene and they rushed a critically injured friend to the Thebe Hospital immediately.

NICK MANIAS: It was dark inside and nobody answered.

They eventually found someone who told them there were no doctors on duty and they needed to drive to Bethlehem, an hour away.

CHRISTA MANIAS: At that stage we started panicking because of this blood running from this person’s head.

This all happened seven years ago…but we went back to Thebe hospital to see what has changed.
Late on a Friday afternoon, one would expect a hospital to be gearing up for a busy weekend.
However, we were met with a desolate waiting area and not a single soul at reception. We explored the hospital for 45 minutes without being challenged, walked into wards and even venturing into the x-ray department.
At casualty we found one nurse and one doctor.

Thebe Hospital is not the only facility with serious problems in what seems to be a collapsing Free State Healthcare system. We found similar, severe problems at Dihlabeng in Bethlehem and Pelonomi in Bloemfontein.


In the Free State Legislature in Bloemfontein this week, the MEC for Health, dr. Benny Malakoane delivered his budget vote speech. He’s very popular amongst his comrades.

DR. BENNY MALAKOANE: I want to state it unequivocally and declare that there is no implosion in the department. The health system is not collapsing.

“DR. ELIZE”: We are getting no support from the department. We are trying to make a difference, but it is getting out of hand and people hold us accountable, people think it is the doctors who don’t have passion.

“DR. JOHN”: The general public must understand that we have to fight for services and it sometimes gets really difficult and it’s just completely exhausting.

The MEC admitted that the department has budgetary constraints because they started the 2014/15 financial year with debt of over a billion rand.

BENNY MALAKOANE: We were faced with a situation where most of the suppliers were reluctant and sometimes refusing to supply medicines and consumables to our facilities and to provide services, particularly to the hospitals.

“DR. JOHN”: You can’t understand how it’s possible that the system doesn’t allow you to manage cases that need urgent management by always just saying: “Oh, but we don’t have money for that.” We, in my opinion, have always been let down by the management of Pelenomi when it comes to some of the emergency activities at the hospital.

We went into Pelonomi Hospital with a hidden camera three times. We found patients in long queues, overflowing bathrooms, no hot water, patients lying on beds in corridors and outside; drips, needles and gloves lying on the floor and blood-stained linen. In the orthopaedic ward, we had free access to patients’ x-rays. Patients there told us they had been waiting for surgery for two months.

This week, Pelonomi was named one of the worst hospitals of nine visited around the country by the Democratic Alliance. They’re now calling for a full-scale investigation, says Mariëtte Pittaway

MARIETTE PITTAWAY/DA: Waste disposal is in rooms behind a burglar proofing window that is standing open.

DEVI: Medical waste?

MARIETTE PITTAWAY: Medical waste.

The National Public Service Commission has recently finalised an investigation into Pelonomi. Dr. Henk Boshoff, who led the investigation, says Pelonomi needs at least a R100 million immediately to fix the situation.

DR. HENK BOSHOFF: The air-conditioning wasn’t working…

DEVI: In the theatre?

DR. HENK BOSHOFF: In one theatre. The generators were installed in 1955, if those generators should break down, it could have serious consequences for the hospital. The boilers were installed in 1995 and the lifespan of a boiler is around 15 years.

Pelenomi said the air-conditioning, lights and anaesthetic machines in theatre work and there are a sufficient number of orthopaedic drills. They also said the PSC investigating team acknowledged that there are good and positive things at the hospital. But dr. Boshoff says time is running out.

DR. HENK BOSHOFF: The budget is just too small to provide an adequate service at Pelenomi. Management told us that 95% of the budget is used for the salaries. They only have 5% available for the provision of the actual service, which is a major concern.

DEVI LINK: In July last year, it was announced that the Free State Department of Health was no longer fit to manage its own budget. Provincial Treasury stepped in. Even the National Minister of Health intervened by rearranging and re-aligning R40 million of the department’s budget.

DR BENNY MALAKOANE: We need to hang tough and tighten our belts without compromising service delivery.

As a result of the budgetary constraints, the ambulance fleet hasn’t been increased since 2010. Only 140 provincial ambulances are available. They need another 130.

RAMCHINDAR SEWPERSAD: We have to call in the private ambulances. Here at Harrismith we run two to three sometimes.

The department managed to outsource 47 ambulances from a private company, Buthelezi at a cost of R6,7 million a month.

DR. BENNY MALAKOANE: In a month Buthelezi does 1200 calls, we do 18 000 a month. Considering the 1200 calls they do a month and the 18 000 we do a month, are they really denting anything?

But this is denting hospitals’ budgets, say doctors at Dihlabeng.

“DR. ELIZE”: It seemed wonderful until we found out that we are literally paying them thousands of rands per transfer.

DEVI: But you were getting that for free before?

“DR. ELIZE”: Yes

DEVI: And it is coming from your hospital budget?

“DR ELIZE”: Yes

DEVI: Is hospital management complaining about this?

“DR. ADRIAN”: Yes

DEVI: To whom?

“DR. ADRIAN:” To management, but they were told that is the way it was done.

DR. BRYCE WICKHAM: Nothing is investigated on merit. It is investigated on who is saying it. You are disciplined very severely if you are in disagreement with what management says.

After many run-ins with management, dr. Wickham chose to resign when questioned about a clinical decision he and a colleague had made.

DR. BRYCE WICKHAM: We were sat down by a member of senior management, basically told it is better to resign than to be fired from the state, because then you lose all your benefits.

Ramchindar claims that when he reported the shortage of life-saving supplies to his management, union and the Health Professions Counsel, his shift leader at the time threatened his life.

RAMCHINDAR SEWPERSAD: The shift leader told me that I will be killed in an accident. The station manager told me that he doesn’t like these things happening to his colleagues, allegations against his colleagues and then I had to sign a written and final warning. I signed it in fear of my life

DR. JOHN: There seems to be a culture of suspension at some of the health institutions in the FS. You get the impression that some of the health personnel get victimised and just gets easily suspended.

Pelonomi has confirmed that two doctors were suspended last year – one of whom has been re-instated.

DR. BENNY MALAKOANE: Some pimps and wimps nicodemously go to the media to reveal certain things that we never denied, and then that comes forward as though we are denying that there are problems in health. We’ve said it. They spread lies, they exaggerate things. You shouldn’t be surprised that the majority of all the people who are always interviewed facelessly on television, it’s those of their ilk.

Some of our sources spoke to us anonymously as they fear being fired.
At great risk of losing his job, Ramchindar spoke to us openly.

RAMCHINDAR SEWPERSAD: What I am doing is in the interest of the poverty stricken, poor people that depend totally on essential services. This is the truth, the truth will surface no matter what.

When we contacted EMS Harrismith’s Station Manager, he referred us to the Free State Health Department. The MEC hasn’t responded to these claims.

MARIETTE PITTAWAY/DA: The MEC, Benny Malakoane does not want to admit that there is a problem.

RAMCHINADAR: He is the Godfather for all these people and these are all his children. He’s got the supply in his hand and if he doesn’t open his hand, his children are going to fade away.

DR JOHN: They are the poorest of the poor. We are definitely letting them down, there is no doubt about it.


ADDITIONAL VOICEOVER:
Three months after being admitted for a broken leg, Kathleen van Heerden died of pulmonary aspiration. Her son, Hendrik said that she wasn’t operated on for a month, there was a broken window in his mother’s room and he warned staff that she would die of lung infection as a result.

This week, Pelonomi said in response that they do not have any records based on scientific evidence that Kathleen suffered lung infection due to a broken window. They also said she couldn’t be operated on earlier because she had developed a haematoma.

Ramchindar claims that when he reported the shortage of life-saving supplies to his management, union and the Health Professions Counsel, his shift leader at the time threatened his life. RAMCHINDAR SEWPERSAD: The shift leader told me that I will be killed in an accident. The station manager told me that he doesn’t like these things happening to his colleagues, allegations against his colleagues and then I had to sign a written and final warning. I signed it in fear of my life DR. JOHN: There seems to be a culture of suspension at some of the health institutions in the FS. You get the impression that some of the health personnel get victimised and just gets easily suspended. Pelonomi has confirmed that two doctors were suspended last year – one of whom has been re-instated. DR. BENNY MALAKOANE: Some pimps and wimps nicodemously go to the media to reveal certain things that we never denied, and then that comes forward as though we are denying that there are problems in health. We’ve said it. They spread lies, they exaggerate things. You shouldn’t be surprised that the majority of all the people who are always interviewed facelessly on television, it’s those of their ilk. Some of our sources spoke to us anonymously as they fear being fired. At great risk of losing his job, Ramchindar spoke to us openly. RAMCHINDAR SEWPERSAD: What I am doing is in the interest of the poverty stricken, poor people that depend totally on essential services. This is the truth, the truth will surface no matter what. When we contacted EMS Harrismith’s Station Manager, he referred us to the Free State Health Department. The MEC hasn’t responded to these claims. MARIETTE PITTAWAY/DA: The MEC, Benny Malakoane does not want to admit that there is a problem. RAMCHINADAR: He is the Godfather for all these people and these are all his children. He’s got the supply in his hand and if he doesn’t open his hand, his children are going to fade away. DR JOHN: They are the poorest of the poor. We are definitely letting them down, there is no doubt about it. ADDITIONAL VOICEOVER: Three months after being admitted for a broken leg, Kathleen van Heerden died of pulmonary aspiration. Her son, Hendrik said that she wasn’t operated on for a month, there was a broken window in his mother’s room and he warned staff that she would die of lung infection as a result. This week, Pelonomi said in response that they do not have any records based on scientific evidence that Kathleen suffered lung infection due to a broken window. They also said she couldn’t be operated on earlier because she had developed a haematoma. metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): When in an accident on the N3 or N5, you will be taken to the Thebe Hospital in Harrismith, medical aid or not. But how equipped is the ambulance that will take you there and the casualty unit?
metadata.Summary: The Free State Department of Health is in a state of collapse. With the MEC of Health in the province boasting that patient care and the safety of patient are his number one priority, patients and doctors on the ground disagree. What they see and experience is not at all the view that the MEC has of what is going on his own department. When in an accident on the N3 or N5, you will be taken to the Thebe Hospital in Harrismith, medical aid or not. But how equipped is the ambulance that will take you there and the casualty unit at Thebe Hospital where you need to be stabilised or treated? It is the only hospital in a 80km radius, yet it is still only a district hospital - with no CT scanner. Our source says he prays that he never has to land up in that hospital. We also again turn our focus to the Free State Health Department's finances - how much wasteful expenditure was there in 2014/2015? And what does the MEC plan to do about the cash-strapped department that doesn't have enough money to provide medicine and basic consumables or cannot repair equipment or infrastructure at failing state hospitals in the province?
metadata.Further information: On Tuesday, MEC Benny Malakoane will deliver his 2015/2016 budget vote speech in the FS legislature. He will say what his plans for the new year are and questions will be asked from the opposition as to how he plans to fix certain problems. The self-confident MEC that said to us he doesn't need someone else to blow his horn, he will do it himself, has some answering to do. His department was found unfit to manage its own finances last year and the management of the financial part of the department was handed over to the Treasury. In this story, we will also go back to all three the hospitals we visited, including Dihlabeng and Pelenomi. The Public Service Commission has just finished an investigation into Pelenomi Hospital and found the the hospital needs at least R100 million immediately to just fix the current problems. It has also found that only 5% of the total financial budget in 2014/15 was spent on actual health care and 95% on salaries. The generators was installed in 1955 and the commissioner of the investigation fears that with constant load shedding the hospital will soon be out of a power back-up. The boilers that warms up the water, was installed in 1995 and only has a life span of 15 years. The hospital has not had hot water for more than a year. Yet, the MEC claims all is well in his department and in his hospitals.
metadata.Expert: Mr. Benny Malakoane FS MEC Health
